editions.note: Themes: an advantage that existed only because a component was expensive, a benchmark mistaken for the problem, and openness that was paid for by reputation. Through-line on purpose: in all three the thing that held the advantage up was never on the invoice. Steered off Ed 75's avoid list -- no design systems or defaults, no commitment or enforcement framing (which is why strangeloopcanon's agent-governance piece and Zvi's 'The Curve Bends You' were both passed over again today, and why spark three is framed on durability of the relationship and recognition rather than on punishment or policing), and no people-versus-systems credit attribution. Roster: zero A-side repeats from the last nine editions. Brian Potter rested since Sep 23, seventeen days, n=1 and that was the Raptor piece, not a display one. Latent Space well last ran Sep 25, fifteen days, and that was Adrian Sanborn, so Pushmeet Kohli is a new who. Seth Godin has been on the ledger once, Sep 21, but only as a B-side framework next to Randy Au -- this is his first appearance as an A-side with a piece actually read. All three B-sides are canonical frameworks never used as a who on the 75-edition ledger: W. Brian Arthur (increasing returns and lock-in, Economic Journal 1989), Russell Ackoff (the error of the third kind, solving the wrong problem well), Robert Axelrod (The Evolution of Cooperation, the shadow of the future). Roster names rested on purpose: Nielsen, Majors and Newton ran Oct 9; Goedecke, Cedric Chin and Orosz Oct 8; Bostian, Ronacher and Randy Au Oct 7; Thompson, Verna and Reis Oct 6. Dunford skipped a fifth edition running. Sources, all fetched by curl via RSS (WebFetch untested again; curl clean on 43 of 45 feeds) and all read in full: construction-physics.com ('The Rise and Fall of the Plasma Screen', Oct 8 -- the Ed 75 earmark, taken as instructed. Read: PLATO needing a display with built-in memory because per-terminal video memory was unaffordable, Bitzer and Willson's 1962 single-cell argon sandwich, the 250,000 resistors a 500x500 screen would have needed, the 1964 move of the electrodes outside the glass, the accidental air leak that produced the memory effect, Owens-Illinois and the 1971 Digivue with PLATO as first customer, then DRAM arriving out of IBM in the late sixties and Moore's Law making the whole memory problem a minor concern. Then the long tail: power-hungry, dimmer, pricier, no robust colour for years; pushed out of laptops by LCD in the nineties; big-screen TV success from Fujitsu's 1990 31-inch through Samsung's 102-inch in 2005; and Potter's own hedge on the ending -- 'the most important issue was likely manufacturing', harder yields and costs than LCD, 'possibly because manufacturers invested far more in LCD manufacturing than they did plasma'. The card keeps that hedge as a hedge. Unused and strong: his closing S-curve-in-reverse frame, and vacuum tubes still made for audio gear as the counter-example of a technology an attribute niche does save -- that is a whole spark against anything on sunsetting a product); latent.space ('Why AlphaFold Didn't Solve Protein Folding', Oct 10, published today, the Biohub x DeepMind panel moderated by Brandon Anderson, read in full from the feed's content:encoded. Read: Anderson opening on whether there is a bitter lesson for data, Sal Candido on scaling laws not being everywhere and the work being to find one, 'I'm lazy, so I'm going to work with what's available', metagenomic sequences that are not even whole proteins still improving a protein language model, Kohli's reading of Rich Sutton as a warning against treating yourself religiously as a modeller or a data person, AlphaFold getting modelling investment because augmenting the PDB was out of reach, inductive bias from biophysics as an unfair advantage, and then the section that carries the spark: proteins are not blocks, they are disordered, shape depends on context, 'we don't know the actual true ground state', what they did was replicate a structure somebody had deposited in the PDB, 'and it just so happens that it's useful'. Unused and strong: the Feynman inversion, creating what we do not understand, which pairs with the Platformer math piece once that becomes readable; Sal's spoke-wheel-bicycle analogy for models of parts versus systems; Kohli on calibration mattering more than interpretability and 'interpretable by whom'; and the 10x-versus-10% closer); seths.blog ('Thin friction and thicker walls', Oct 9, read in full, 1,092 characters -- the thin friction of not yelling in the library, agents and cheap bots that multiply exponentially, care little about being shunned and have no interest in reputation, fake sincerity now cheap, interchangeable identities subverting a tradition of owning your words, and the close: you won't be able to knock unless you're invited, and the invitation will probably be filtered out. His 'Our genie problem', Oct 8, was read too and left unused; 'Uniformity', Oct 3, stays held because it is a companion to Ed 75's HOA spark). Verification discipline: Arthur's 1989 paper confirmed by search before writing -- Economic Journal 99(394), lock-in to a path 'not necessarily efficient' by small historical events, an early lead cornering the market -- so the card claims path dependence and not that the market always picks the loser. Axelrod grounded in his own words, not a summary: fetched his Breakthrough chapter and used 'the importance of the next encounter between the same two individuals', 'the foundation of cooperation is not really trust, but the durability of the relationship', and the requirement that a strategy discriminate between those who reciprocate and those who do not. Ackoff is the one soft spot and it is handled: searches could not find a primary source for 'we fail more often because we solve the wrong problem', which circulates via quote aggregators, and the error of the third kind traces to Kimball 1957 and Mitroff and Featheringham 1974, so the card paraphrases his documented position and quotes nothing. Pairings Brian Potter x W. Brian Arthur, Pushmeet Kohli x Russell Ackoff, Seth Godin x Robert Axelrod, all three checked programmatically against the full 75-edition pairing set and all three new. Best unused on the shelf, in order: nngroup 'Context Libraries: How AI Power Users Manage Context Engineering' (Oct 9, and the sister piece 'The New Siri's Biggest Strength Is Not Intelligence' same day -- held only because the nngroup well ran Oct 4 with Tanner Kohler, so good from about Oct 12 and it is the most directly useful pair on the shelf for someone shipping agents); platformer 'AI is solving math problems faster than humans can understand the solutions' (Oct 9, now live on the web and the Ed 75 retry worked -- but Platformer ran yesterday, so hold it two or three days, and when it runs, pair it with the Feynman inversion from today's spark two rather than with anything on caps); leaddev 'Your junior engineers are getting faster but are they getting better?' and 'Software developers are becoming agent builders' (both Oct 8, leaddev ran Oct 7); jim-nielsen 'Getting off the Modernization Treadmill' (Oct 8, his notes on Alexander Petros's Big Sky DevCon talk -- now two Nielsens back to back on the ledger, so hold to about Oct 14); pragmaticengineer 'The Pulse: internal vibe-coding apps' (Oct 8, well ran Oct 8); interconnects 'I expect rapid progress but not towards general superintelligence' (Oct 9, Nathan Lambert rested since Sep 20 -- read the free portion in full and it is strong: superhuman GPU engineers making research cheap, 'an era where good ideas can be much more valuable than good execution in software', Jevons for agents, Meta's Muse as value from understanding agents rather than pushing the frontier, and RL-environment data quality as industrial-scale low-hanging fruit. Passed over today only because it rhymes with spark one on commoditisation; take it within the week, it is paywalled past the RL-environments section so author off the free portion); strangeloopcanon 'Agent governance looks less like moral education and more like institutional economics' (Oct 6, now twice deferred on the enforcement avoid -- Ed 75's avoid list expires with this edition, so it is clear to run from tomorrow); thezvi 'The Curve Bends You' (Oct 7, same deferral, same release). Retired: the interconnected.org 'What we're building at Inanimate' earmark, as Ed 75 instructed to take it or retire it -- fetched and read, it is a weeknote pointing at three YouTube videos, and the one real idea in it ('Why an Anything Device Needs a Familiar Shape', plus Webb's obsession with the egg timer shaped like an egg) lives inside the video, not the post, so there is nothing readable to anchor a spark on. Matt Webb is worth keeping as a who; watch interconnected.org for a real post. Feed notes: aprildunford.com?format=rss and melissaperri.com?format=rss both return malformed XML now (invalid token and undefined entity respectively) -- parse them leniently or scrape the index. brianbalfour.com/feed still 404s, use /essays. randsinrepose.com/feed/ still 403s. platformer.news web pages are readable again for the Oct 9 piece, so the gating is inconsistent rather than permanent; try the page and fall back to the feed. Avoid tomorrow: commoditisation and what gets cheap next, benchmarks and evals, and anything resting on identity, reputation or trust. Hshop and Nshop untouched.

editions.note: Themes: a standards catalogue shipped without its generative sequence, a cap whose enforcement machinery does not exist, and credit read off the ten percent a leader controls. Through-line chosen on purpose: in all three the structure had already decided and the surface got the attention. Steered off Ed 74's avoid list -- no reading or reviewing code, no pace layers or fast-versus-slow change, no capital structure or balance-sheet framing. Roster: zero A-side B-sides, all three partners are canonical frameworks never used as a who on the 74-edition ledger -- Christopher Alexander (A Pattern Language, the late-70s self-critique, generative sequence over static catalogue), Thomas Schelling (The Strategy of Conflict 1960, commitment binds by visibly surrendering the option, not by sincerity), Richard Hackman with Ruth Wageman (sixty thirty ten: prework, launch, live coaching). A-sides rested: Jim Nielsen last ran Sep 22 and Sep 29, seventeen and ten days, n=2 going in; Charity Majors Sep 22, seventeen days, n=1; Casey Newton and the Platformer well Oct 1, eight days, n=1. Roster names rested on purpose: Goedecke, Cedric Chin and Orosz ran Oct 8; Bostian, Ronacher and Randy Au Oct 7; Thompson, Verna and Reis Oct 6; Baschez, Hochstein and Tunguz Oct 5. Dunford skipped a fourth edition running, positioning-as-context has run Sep 17, 19, 23, 24 and 28. Deming rested, ran Oct 5, and he was the obvious alternative B-side for spark three -- Hackman was chosen over him precisely to keep Deming's ninety-four percent out of the room two editions later. Sources, all fetched by curl (WebFetch untested again this run; curl clean on 38 of 40 feeds and pages) and all read in full: blog.jim-nielsen.com ('Apple's App Icon HOA', Oct 6 -- the Ed 74 earmark, taken as instructed, and the Alexander pairing was already half-done by that note: Louie Mantia's squircle history, paving the cowpaths because most icons are brand logos now, Icon Composer and the glass effects as default-good tooling, 'some of the platform's best icons look worse while some of the worst look better', floor up and ceiling down, the HOA where nothing is a dump and nobody stands out. Note the live URL is /2026/app-icon-hoa/, not /2026/apple-app-icon-hoa/ which 404s -- Ed 74's note had the slug slightly wrong); patternlanguage.com/archive/ieee.html (Alexander's 1996 OOPSLA keynote, fetched and read for the B-side rather than quoted from memory -- and it paid: his own words are 'the buildings generated were okay, but not profound', isolated features improved while the whole lacked coherent living structure, 'whatever was going wrong wasn't going to be corrected by writing a few more patterns', and in Part C the admission that the sequential use 'dropped into the background' because the 1960s effort went entirely onto the individual patterns, leaving the published language 'static'. Unused and strong: the fifteen recursive geometric properties, and the Part C argument that computer scientists should inherit responsibility for generating living structure because the generative process is native to them -- that is a whole spark against anyone on agents); platformer.news ('Does intelligence need a hard cap?', Oct 7, read in full from the RSS content:encoded because the web page is gated to the nav -- The Curve in Berkeley under Chatham House Rule, multiple speakers floating a limit on how intelligent a system may become, Amodei's 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement, responsible scaling policies, compute and self-copy limits, the admission that no enforcement capability exists at lab or country level, the US government opposing it, the 'morally binding' accord signed with the president, and the OpenAI-Hugging Face fallout as one of two reasons the mood shifted. Unused: the embedded-evaluators line, which collides with Ed 64's Zvi piece, and the antitrust-waiver idea); charity.wtf ('If your team is happy, are you doing a good job?', Oct 8, part 3 of her dialogue with Cat Hicks -- Project Aristotle's five dynamics and DORA, the brilliant-jerk era, psychological safety unmoored from accountability and from learning, 'if your team is happy you're doing a good job' as ZIRP-era management, eudaimonia against hedonic pleasure, Gilbert and Kahneman on predicting our own happiness, 'you can't tell from the calendar invite' on learning spend, and the closer: we credit people for what structures do. Unused and strong: 'you can't tell from the calendar invite' is a complete spark on its own against anything on leading indicators; so is her line that the second most effective leaders are crappy humans who are skilled operators). Hackman's sixty thirty ten was verified by search rather than asserted, and the sources disagree on whether the split is shares of a leader's contribution or shares of variance in team performance -- the card says leader's contribution and calls the numbers a rough heuristic, which is the defensible reading. Same discipline on Alexander: the search warned that no source supports calling his pattern work a 'failure', so the card uses his own 'okay, but not profound'. Pairings Jim Nielsen x Christopher Alexander, Casey Newton x Thomas Schelling, Charity Majors x Richard Hackman, all three checked programmatically against the full 74-edition pairing set and all three new.
